introduction: The Misha Browser extension (`src/extension/manifest.json`) asks for the permissions below. The extension has no backend of its own and loads no remote code. Everything it returns goes to the native messaging host on the user's own Mac. The Slack Web API calls and file downloads it makes run inside the user's signed-in Slack page and go to the workspace's address on Slack's domain and to `files.slack.com`. A file upload goes to the upload URL that Slack's Web API answered for it, whose host the extension does not check.

The extension does two jobs. Its Slack transport reads new messages in the user's signed-in Slack tab and makes allowlisted Slack Web API calls there for the Misha app. Its tab commands let the browser tools of misha-browser's MCP server (`tab_*`) read and drive the user's tabs.
singlePurpose: Misha Browser connects AI agents that run on the user's own Mac to the user's signed-in browser, so they can read pages and carry out the browser actions the user asks for. Misha's Slack transport is one such use: it reads new messages in the user's signed-in Slack tab and makes allowlisted Slack calls there for the Misha app. Both uses reach the browser through one native messaging host on the same Mac.

nativeMessaging.capability: Exchanges messages with the native messaging host `misha.browser_bridge`, a program the user installs on their own Mac.
nativeMessaging.justification: Every request reaches the extension this way: the Misha app's Slack requests and the browser tools' tab commands. Replies, new Slack messages and the extension's status go back the same way. The extension has no backend of its own, so nothing on the Mac could reach it otherwise.

collectionTiming.detail: The extension connects when it starts and keeps the connection open. New Slack messages and status go to the listening process as they happen; everything else goes only as the reply to a request.

limits: The extension connects to no other native host, and the host's registration lets only this extension start it.
The host only relays: it passes messages between the extension and processes of the same user on the same Mac (the Misha app, misha-browser's MCP server) and stores none of them.
With no process listening, the host drops events and status. The extension keeps the events in its pending queue (see `unlimitedStorage`).

scripting.capability: Runs the extension's own bundled functions, and its bundled relay script, in a tab: in the page's own world or in the extension's isolated world.
scripting.justification: In a signed-in Slack tab it reads which workspace and user the tab is signed in as, from Slack's saved client state, and makes the allowlisted Slack Web API calls, file downloads and uploads the Misha app asks for. After the extension reloads or updates, it injects the extension's own relay script again into each open Slack tab whose relay the browser has cut off, so capture goes on without reloading the tab (see the content scripts below). It first checks, in the extension's isolated world, that the tab's top document is a page on `https://app.slack.com` with no relay of the running extension, and injects into that document only, never into a page the tab navigated to meanwhile. In the tab a browser tool names, it reads the page as an outline of its text and controls (`tab_read`, `tab_find`), finds where a control sits so the tool can click or type into it, reads a form field's state, selects a field's content before typing replaces it, picks an option in a select, reports where the pointer is and whether the page has focus, and waits until the page stops changing after an action.

collectionTiming.detail: On Slack tabs it runs without a request: the relay check when the service worker starts, and the account read for each new message and, while a process listens, whenever the extension reports its status (a listener attaching, a Slack tab loading or closing, a change in a tab's capture or in the queue). Slack calls, downloads and uploads run only when the Misha app asks for one. Page commands run only when a browser tool asks, but the pointer listener that locating a target or taking a screenshot starts in a page keeps running after the tool finishes (see limits).

limits: Everything it runs is part of the extension's package; no code comes from the network or the native host.

The function that runs in Slack's page returns only the account's ids and the workspace's name, Slack's answers, file bytes or an uploaded file's id. It does not return the saved session token, though Chrome exposes the token it sends to the service worker temporarily, for redaction (see `webRequest` and Where Slack's credentials go).

Slack calls are limited to the Web API methods listed under Slack transport limits. A download is fetched only from `files.slack.com`, with redirects refused. An upload's bytes go to the upload URL Slack's answer names, whose host the extension does not check and whose redirects it follows (see Where Slack's credentials go).
Page commands run in the extension's isolated world and read the page's DOM only: not a page's localStorage, Slack's saved session or the cookie store.

When page commands walk the page for an outline or a search, they skip script and head content, hidden inputs and elements the page does not show. That filter decides which elements the walk visits, not what a visited element can reveal. A visible label whose control the page hides (a styled checkbox) is listed with that control's role, name and current state, so the value of a text field the page hides can appear in an ordinary outline, a password field's still only as filled or empty. A control's name can also come from label or `aria-labelledby` text the page hides. A ref the walk handed out keeps working while its element stays in the page, even after the page hides it, and a field read through that ref returns the field's current value, hidden or not. Reading the region of a ref lists the control the ref names without checking its visibility.

A password field's value comes back only as filled or empty in an outline, or as its length in a field read. A field read, which the typing tools make while they type, still reads the raw value: the extension keeps the last value it read from each password field in the page's isolated world, to tell whether the value changed between reads, and keeps it until a later read of that field replaces it or the document unloads. The page's own scripts cannot see the isolated world.

The first time a browser tool locates a target in a page, which clicks, drags, scrolling, typing into a referenced field and screenshots do, the extension starts listening for mouse movement in that document and keeps listening until the document unloads, whether or not a tool is acting. Key presses, picking an option and typing into the focused element do not start it. It keeps only the latest pointer position and a count of moves, not a history, and sends them only when a browser tool asks for them while it moves the pointer.

Before a click, a drag, a key press, picking an option, or typing that submits or goes to the focused element, the extension records the page's outline (its text, controls and ordinary field values, with a password field only as filled or empty) and its unredacted URL in the service worker's memory, to report what the action changed. The record stays until another of those actions in that tab records a new one, the tab closes or the service worker stops. Opening or navigating to a page, reading it, scrolling and typing into a referenced field without submitting do not replace it, so the record of a page can stay after the tab has left it.

A downloaded Slack file's bytes stay in the service worker's memory until the Misha app pulls the last chunk, and an upload's chunks until the app asks to prepare the upload. Neither has a timeout: a transfer the app abandons stays until the service worker stops, and closing the Slack tab or disconnecting the app does not clear it.
While the connection to the native host is open, Chrome keeps the service worker running, so what stays in its memory until the worker stops can stay for as long as the browser runs.

alarms.capability: Wakes the service worker every 30 seconds.
alarms.justification: On each alarm the extension reconnects to the native messaging host when the connection is down, for example before the user has installed the host or after it stopped.

collectionTiming.detail: The alarm fires on its schedule. It carries no data.

limits: While the connection is open, the alarm does nothing.

unlimitedStorage.capability: Exempts the extension's own storage from Chrome's quota and from eviction under storage pressure.
unlimitedStorage.justification: The Slack transport keeps its pending queue in IndexedDB, in the extension's own origin: each new Slack message waits there until the Misha app confirms it saved it, so a message the database stored survives a service worker or browser restart. Without this permission Chrome may evict the extension's IndexedDB under storage pressure, taking the queued messages and the count of lost ones with it.

collectionTiming.detail: A new message is stored as soon as a Slack tab's capture hands it over, and removed when the Misha app acknowledges it, which the app does only after saving it on its side. While writes to the database fail, a new message is held in the service worker's memory instead and forwarded from there without being stored.

limits: The durable queue holds at most 2000 pending events. When it is full, a new event is not stored: it is counted as lost, and the Misha app sees the count in the extension's status.

While writes to the database fail, the extension holds new events in the service worker's memory, up to a separate limit of 2000, and forwards them from there. An event past that limit is lost, and its loss is counted in memory only. The status reports the failure, the number of held events and that in-memory count.

The first write that succeeds after a failure stores the held events the Misha app has not acknowledged yet, as far as the durable queue has room. It counts the rest as lost, and adds the in-memory count to the stored one.
A service worker or browser restart while writes fail loses every held event the Misha app has not acknowledged, and the in-memory count of lost ones, with no record of either.
A stored event has no age limit. It stays, and is forwarded again, until the Misha app acknowledges it.
A stored event holds the account it came to and the message cut down to the fields listed under Slack transport limits.
Nothing else is written to disk: the network log (see `webRequest`), page outlines and file transfers (see `scripting`) stay in the service worker's memory.

tabs.capability: Reads every open tab's title and URL, and opens, focuses and closes tabs.
tabs.justification: `tab_list` lists the open tabs with their titles and URLs, and `tab_open`, `tab_switch` and `tab_close` open, focus and close tabs. The Slack transport uses it to find the open Slack tabs and to report its status again when one loads or closes.

collectionTiming.detail: Tab titles and URLs leave the extension only in the reply to a browser tool. The Slack transport finds the Slack tabs without a request, and reports for each only the account it is signed in as and how its capture stands.

limits: Each structured URL field a tab command returns (a tab's, a page's or a download's) goes through the name- and pattern-based redaction described under `webRequest`, which also removes a URL's userinfo and the grant in Slack's upload URLs.
An opaque link that grants access under an ordinary name passes unchanged, and a URL that appears in page text or a field value comes back as the page shows it.

webRequest.capability: Observes the fetch and XHR requests every tab sends: method, URL, request body, request headers (cookies included) and the status or error that ends each one.
webRequest.justification: `tab_network` lists a tab's requests so the model can learn the API a web app calls, and the action tools wait for the requests an action started before they read the page again.

collectionTiming.detail: Observation does not wait for a tool: the service worker records every tab's fetch and XHR requests for as long as it runs, whether or not a browser tool is in use. A tab's log leaves the extension only when `tab_network` asks for it.

limits: It only observes, and never blocks or changes a request.

Chrome exposes each request's body and headers, credentials included, to the service worker temporarily, for redaction. It redacts them before it records the request: a body field, query parameter or header named like a token, password, secret, API key, authorization or cookie, and any value shaped like a known token or key, is replaced with `[redacted]`. Matched credential values are replaced before storage; an unrecognized credential can remain.
The redaction looks for credentials only. The rest of a body is recorded as the page sent it, so personal, health, financial or location data a site posts in a request is kept as it is.
The log holds the latest 200 requests per tab and a request body up to 20,000 characters, and never stores response bodies.

The log lives only in the service worker's memory and is never written to disk. A tab's log goes when the tab closes, and the whole log goes when the service worker stops, which an open connection to the native host can put off for as long as the browser runs.
Requests no tab sent, such as the browser's own or another extension's, are not recorded.

downloads.justification: After a browser tool's action, the extension reports the downloads started since the action began (each one's URL, local filename, state, bytes received and any error), so the tool can tell the model that a click downloaded a file, whether it finished, and whether the browser waits for the user to choose where to save it.

collectionTiming.detail: After a browser tool's action, never on its own. The extension listens for no download events.

limits: The search covers the whole browser, not only the tab the action ran in, so a download started elsewhere in that time is reported too.
A download's URL goes through the name- and pattern-based redaction described under `webRequest`, which can leave an unrecognized credential.
The extension only searches the download list. It never starts, opens or deletes a download.

<all_urls>.capability: Gives the extension access to every site: to script any page, to observe any page's requests with `webRequest`, and to capture the visible part of a tab.
<all_urls>.justification: The browser tools work on whatever site the user has open, so the sites cannot be named in advance. The tools read and drive a page with `scripting`, and `tab_screenshot` captures the visible part of a tab.

collectionTiming.detail: A page's content and screenshots are read only when a browser tool asks. Request observation under `webRequest` runs on every site without a request. The Slack transport's capture in Slack tabs is described under the content scripts below.

limits: Page text, control names, ordinary field values and screenshots come back as the page shows them, including any credential, personal, health, financial or location data the page displays.
The extension reads the localStorage of no page but Slack's, where its own code reads only the saved client state, and it never reads the cookie store.

observer.js.capability: Watches Slack's own real-time socket. It passes each new message to the relay, cut down to the fields the Misha app reads (listed under Slack transport limits), with the account the tab showed when it came, and reports whether the socket is open. It reads the signed-in user's id from Slack's saved client state to key each message.
observer.js.justification: Slack's web client receives new messages on this socket, and the Misha app needs them as they arrive to answer in Slack. The script runs before Slack's own scripts so it can watch the socket Slack opens.

collectionTiming.detail: Without a request, while a Slack tab is open: each new message is passed on as it arrives. Edits and deletions are not passed on.

limits: It sends nothing on Slack's socket and never passes on the socket's address, which holds a token.
Nothing else the page received leaves it, such as file URLs, profiles or message formatting.
Message text goes on as written, including any credential someone wrote into a message.
It holds up to 50 messages no relay has taken yet, such as those that come while the extension reloads, in the page's memory, and hands them to the next relay; past that the oldest is dropped.

relay.js.capability: Takes a private channel from the observer, checks every message on it against the protocol's shapes, and forwards new messages and the socket's state to the service worker.
relay.js.justification: A script in the page's own world has no channel to the extension, so the observer needs a partner in the extension's world. Checking what the observer sends keeps anything outside the fixed shapes from reaching the extension.

collectionTiming.detail: Without a request, while a Slack tab is open. When the extension reloads or updates, the browser cuts the relay in every open tab off from the extension and loads the manifest's scripts only into pages that load afterwards, so the service worker injects the relay again into each open Slack tab (see `scripting`). There it takes a new channel from the observer, which has kept watching the socket and held any new message that came while no relay ran.

limits: It takes a channel only in the top frame of a page on `https://app.slack.com`.
It passes on nothing that does not match the protocol's shapes, and reports the tab's capture as failed instead.

Re-attaching works for pages that loaded with this version of the observer. A page still running an older version captures again only once the tab reloads, so upgrading from such a build needs each open Slack tab reloaded once.

nativeMessaging: The native messaging host is part of this repository (`src/host/`). The user installs it on their own Mac, and the installer registers it as `misha.browser_bridge` with Chrome, Brave or both, naming only this extension's id as allowed to start it. The browser starts the host when the extension connects.

The host relays between the extension and processes of the same user on the same Mac, over a socket in a folder only that user can open: the Misha app and misha-browser's MCP server connect there. Requests come in from those processes and replies go back to the process that asked. New Slack messages and status go to the one process that listens for them, and its acknowledgements go back to the extension. The host keeps none of it.
A request names a method from the extension's fixed set of handlers and carries data as its parameters. It never carries code, and a method the extension does not know is answered with an error.

remoteCode.statement: Every script the extension runs is in its package: the service worker, the two content scripts and the functions it injects with `scripting`, bundled from this repository's source without minification. The extension evaluates no string as code, and its schema library runs in its mode that generates no code. Requests from the native host name a method and carry data, never code. Slack messages and page content are data and never run as script.

categories.detail: The Slack account's team and user ids and the workspace's name, and whatever Slack's answers, the request bodies the network observer records and the pages a browser tool reads hold, such as names and email addresses in Slack profiles or in a form a site posts.

The extension does not look for health data, but it handles any that appears in what it collects for other purposes: the fetch and XHR request bodies every tab sends, which the network observer records on every site without a request and filters for credentials only; the page text, field values and screenshots a browser tool reads; and Slack messages and files. A diagnosis in a form a site posts, for example, is recorded as sent.

The extension does not look for financial or payment data, but it handles any that appears in what it collects for other purposes: the fetch and XHR request bodies every tab sends, which the network observer records on every site without a request and filters for credentials only; the page text, field values and screenshots a browser tool reads; and Slack messages and files. A card number in a checkout form a site posts, for example, is recorded as sent unless it sits under a credential-like name.

The Slack page command reads Slack's session token from Slack's saved client state inside the page, sends it with the requests the Misha app asks for, and does not return it. Chrome exposes every outgoing request's credentials (tokens, cookies, passwords in request bodies), Slack's token and cookie included, to the service worker temporarily, for redaction: it redacts the ones it recognizes before recording, and records an unrecognized one as sent. When a typing tool reads a password field, the extension returns only the value's length, but keeps the last raw value it read from that field in the page's isolated world until a later read replaces it or the document unloads. A credential a page displays comes back in page reads and screenshots.
New messages in the user's signed-in Slack tab, the Slack messages and files the Misha app reads or sends through Slack's Web API, and any messages on a page a browser tool reads.

The extension asks for no geolocation permission and reads no device location. It still handles location that appears in what it collects for other purposes: coordinates or an address in the fetch and XHR request bodies every tab sends, which the network observer records on every site without a request and filters for credentials only; a map or an address on a page a browser tool reads or screenshots; a place in a tab's or a request's URL; and a place someone names in a Slack message.
The open tabs' titles and URLs, returned when a browser tool asks, and the URLs of the fetch and XHR requests tabs send, recorded without a request and kept in memory.

Network monitoring: the fetch and XHR requests every tab sends, recorded without a request and kept in memory. Mouse movement: from the first time a browser tool locates a target in a page (a click, drag, scroll, typing into a referenced field or a screenshot), the extension keeps the latest pointer position in that document and a count of moves, not a history, until the document unloads, whether or not a tool is acting, and sends them only when a browser tool asks. The extension installs no click or keyboard listeners, though what the user typed reaches it in request bodies and field values.

Page text, controls, form field state, screenshots and the browser's download list, when a browser tool asks; the page outline recorded before a click, drag, key press, option pick, or typing that submits or goes to the focused element, kept until another of those actions in the tab records a new one, the tab closes or the service worker stops, so navigating and scrolling leave it in place; and the bytes of Slack files the Misha app downloads or uploads, kept until the transfer completes or the service worker stops.

dataUsage.recipients: The extension sends data only to the native messaging host on the user's own Mac, which passes it to the Misha app or misha-browser's MCP server there. Its Slack Web API calls go only to the workspace's https address on Slack's domain and its file downloads only to `files.slack.com`, both with redirects refused. A file upload's bytes go to the upload URL Slack's `files.getUploadURLExternal` answer names: the extension does not check that URL's host and follows its redirects. The Misha app and the MCP server give the data to the AI agent working on the user's request; the privacy policy describes where the agent's data goes from there.
certifications: User data is not sold to third parties.
User data is not used or transferred for purposes unrelated to the single purpose above.
User data is not used or transferred to determine creditworthiness or for lending purposes.
dataUsage.limitedUse: The use of data the extension handles complies with the Chrome Web Store User Data Policy, including the Limited Use requirements.

paragraphs: The function the service worker injects into a Slack tab's own page (`src/service-worker/slack-page.ts`) is the only code that uses the Slack session token. For each call the Misha app asks for, it reads the token from Slack's saved client state, adds it to the request, and sends that request only to the workspace's https address on Slack's domain, with redirects refused. A private file is fetched only from `files.slack.com`, with the browser's cookies and no token, and redirects refused. An upload is different: its bytes go, without the token, to the `upload_url` in Slack's `files.getUploadURLExternal` answer, with the browser's default request settings. The extension checks only that the URL is a string, not its host, and follows redirects; the browser sends cookies only when the URL is on the page's own origin, and Slack's usual upload URL, on `files.slack.com`, is not. It returns the account's ids and the workspace's name, Slack's answer, file bytes or an uploaded file's id. It does not return the token it reads from Slack's saved client state, though a credential someone wrote into a message or a file comes back like any other content. Slack's answers and file bytes go on as Slack sent them, without credential filtering. A command that fails returns a fixed failure code, so no error message can quote what the page holds.

The script that watches Slack's socket reads only the signed-in user's id from the saved state and never passes on the socket's address, which holds a token. It sends only whether the socket is open and new messages cut down to fixed fields, with the account the tab showed. Message text goes on as written. Its partner script and the service worker reject anything outside those shapes. The native host passes messages between the extension and processes on the same Mac and keeps nothing.

The exception is `webRequest`. Chrome exposes the body and headers of every fetch and XHR request a tab sends, Slack's included, to the service worker temporarily, for redaction, so the token in the `token` field of Slack's API calls and the session cookie in the `Cookie` header reach it. It redacts both before it records the request, so `tab_network` shows them as `[redacted]`, and neither is stored or sent to the native host.
tabCommandReturns: The page commands behind `tab_read`, `tab_find` and field reads run in the extension's isolated world and read the page's DOM. They do not read Slack's saved session, a page's localStorage or the cookie store. Their walk of the page skips script and head content, hidden inputs and elements the page does not show, but a visible label lists the current state of the hidden control it stands for, a hidden text field's value included, a control's name can come from label text the page hides, and a ref the walk handed out keeps reading its element after the page hides it (see `scripting`). They give a password field's value only as filled or empty in an outline, or as its length in a field read, while keeping the last raw value of a field read in the page's isolated world (see `scripting`). Page text, control names and ordinary field values come back as the page shows them, so a credential the page displays, or one pasted into a Slack message, comes back too.
`tab_screenshot` returns the pixels the tab shows, including any credential on screen.
Network requests and returned URLs are redacted by name and pattern only. An opaque credential under an ordinary name, such as the key in a share link, comes back unchanged.
credentialHandling.outOfScope: Scripts that already run in the Slack page (Slack's own code, or another extension's) are out of scope: they hold the session themselves. The README's Security section states this threat model.
